title: Housing exclusion is a layered pathway shaped by poverty, housing markets, institutional transitions, relationships, health and hidden forms of insecurity
source_unit: OECD, What is driving homelessness and housing exclusion in OECD and EU countries? A review of the literature and cross-national data
geography: OECD and EU countries, with cross-national evidence from the 2023 EU-SILC special module and the 2022 Canadian Housing Survey

structural_drivers.value: poverty and adverse economic conditions are consistently identified as fundamental contributors, with housing costs, shortages of affordable or social housing and eviction risks important in some contexts

systemic_drivers.value: poorly managed transitions from care, prisons and other institutions can contribute to pathways into homelessness

relational_drivers.value: family conflict, relationship breakdown and intimate-partner violence can act as pathways, while poor health often increases vulnerability rather than acting alone

observations.method: Review of academic literature combined with cross-national analysis of housing-difficulty and homelessness data.
observations.uncertainty: The paper synthesizes heterogeneous studies and definitions; it does not provide a single causal model or comparable effect size for every pathway across countries.
observations.subgroup: People facing poverty, housing-cost pressure, eviction, institutional discharge, family conflict, violence, health constraints, youth transition or weak social support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Individual and relational factors matter, but focusing on them alone can obscure the structural and institutional conditions that make a crisis translate into loss of housing.

observations.period: 2026 publication; hidden homelessness and measurement visibility

hidden_forms.value: temporary stays with family or friends because of lack of housing are less visible and under-researched, yet more widespread in the reviewed survey evidence than rough sleeping or shelter stays

definition_problem.value: there is no internationally harmonized definition of homelessness, housing exclusion or housing difficulties

ethos_scope.value: the paper uses the ETHOS Light typology to distinguish rough sleeping, emergency accommodation, homeless accommodation, institutions, non-conventional dwellings and temporary stays with family or friends

observations.method: Comparison of official statistics, survey measures and the ETHOS Light living-situation framework.
observations.uncertainty: Hidden homelessness has no single formal definition, and country statistics differ in which living situations they include; apparent cross-country differences may partly reflect measurement design.
observations.subgroup: People staying temporarily with family or friends, in unsuitable housing, in institutions, in non-conventional dwellings or outside visible shelter systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Broadening the definition improves visibility, but it can reduce comparability if classifications are not operationalized consistently and may complicate targeting of limited prevention resources.

observations.period: 2026 publication; EU-SILC and Canadian survey evidence

lifetime_housing_difficulty.value: approximately 5% of the EU population reported having experienced some form of housing difficulty over their lifetime, rising to 8–10% in several countries

current_vs_lifetime.value: lifetime housing-difficulty measures are much larger than national point-in-time estimates that typically place current homelessness below 1%

canada_hidden_ratio.value: among Canadian respondents, temporary stays with family or friends were four times more likely than past rough sleeping or emergency/temporary shelter stays

observations.method: Analysis of the 2023 EU-SILC special module on housing difficulties and the 2022 Canadian Housing Survey; the two sources are not directly comparable in every respect.
observations.uncertainty: These are survey-based lifetime or past-experience measures, not current prevalence; recall, wording, coverage and country-specific definitions affect the estimates.
observations.subgroup: People with past housing difficulty, people who stayed with family or friends, and people who experienced rough sleeping or shelter use.
observations.counterinterpretation: A lifetime measure captures cumulative exposure that point-in-time counts miss, but it should not be interpreted as the share currently needing housing or as a direct measure of policy failure.

entry.value: family or relationship breakdown is frequently cited alongside financial problems, housing-market pressure and other unspecified causes

exit_variation.value: access to housing is critical for people in severe situations, while employment plays a larger role for those staying with family or friends

support_route.value: family and friends can both be part of hidden housing insecurity and a source of support that helps people exit it

observations.method: Synthesis of cross-national survey results and literature on pathways into and out of housing difficulty.
observations.uncertainty: The paper identifies associations and pathway differences; it does not establish that employment or housing access alone causes durable exits for all groups.
observations.subgroup: People in severe homelessness, people temporarily housed with family or friends, people seeking work, households experiencing relationship breakdown and people with limited support networks.
observations.counterinterpretation: Employment and social support can stabilize housing, but insecure work, unaffordable rents, violence, health needs or institutional barriers can prevent those routes from producing durable security.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD DOI for Working Paper No. 336.

boundary: This record adds a housing and household-security signal linking homelessness and housing exclusion to poverty, housing affordability, eviction, institutional transitions, relationships, health, employment, social support and measurement visibility. It is a literature review and cross-national survey synthesis, not a harmonized current prevalence census, a single causal model, or a direct evaluation of any housing policy.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD publication page and downloadable working paper were reviewed for structural, systemic, individual and relational drivers; hidden homelessness; ETHOS Light classification; EU-SILC and Canadian survey contrasts; and entry/exit pathways.
